definition: A name attached to a value with `=`, such as `unit_price = 39`, so the value can be used later; the right side is computed first, then the name points at the result.
The data type shared by every value in a pandas column, such as `int64`, `float64`, `object` (text), `bool` or `datetime64`; a wrong dtype is behind many data bugs.
A Python container of key: value pairs, such as a product's name mapped to its price; you look values up by key with `d[key]` or `d.get(key, default)`.
A one-line way to build a list, `[expr for x in items if condition]`, that applies an expression to each item and optionally filters which items are kept.
A string literal prefixed with `f` that embeds values in braces with optional formatting, such as `f"{revenue:,.2f}"` for 1,234.50 or `f"{share:.1%}"` for 12.5%.
The report Python prints when an exception stops a program; read it from the bottom, where the last line names the error type and message, then up to the failing line.
A one-dimensional pandas array of values with an index of labels; a single column of a DataFrame is a Series.
The pandas table: columns that are Series sharing one row index, with methods to load, select, filter, group, join and reshape data.
pandas' rule that operations between two Series or DataFrames match values by index label, not by position; labels present on only one side produce NaN.
The two precise selectors in pandas: `.loc[rows, columns]` selects by label and includes the end of a slice, while `.iloc` selects by integer position and excludes it.
A Series of True and False values, usually from a comparison, used to select rows with `df[mask]`; its sum counts matches and its mean gives their share.
Assigning through two selections, such as `df["col"][mask] = value`; it may change a temporary copy instead of the DataFrame, so use one `.loc` call instead.
pandas behaviour, default from version 3.0 and optional in 2.x, in which every selection acts as a copy, so the only way to change a DataFrame is to assign to it directly.
Short for not a number: the classic pandas marker for a missing value in float columns; it is not equal to anything, so test for it with `isna()`.
A pandas dtype such as `Int64`, `Float64`, `boolean` or `string` that stores missing values as `pd.NA`, so integer columns stay integers even with gaps.
The `.str` attribute of a text Series that applies string methods such as `strip`, `title`, `replace`, `split` and `contains` to every value at once.
A pattern language for text in which characters like `$` and `.` have special meanings; pass `regex=False` to treat them as plain characters.
A date string such as 05/08/2025 that is valid under both day-first and month-first readings; only outside information can decide which one is correct.
An `assert condition, message` statement that does nothing when the condition holds and stops the program with the message when it fails; used to state what clean data must look like.
The pandas operation that splits rows into groups by key, applies a calculation to each group and combines the results into one table.
A form of `agg` in which each keyword names an output column and its value is a (column, function) pair, such as `revenue=("revenue", "sum")`.
The pandas method that combines two tables side by side by matching key values; `how` sets the join type and `validate` checks the expected key relationship.
The rule for unmatched keys in a merge: inner keeps keys found on both sides, left keeps every left row, right every right row, and outer keeps all keys.
Two shapes for the same data: long has one row per observation, wide spreads one variable across columns; `pivot_table` goes from long to wide and `melt` back.
A pandas method that groups rows with a datetime index into regular periods such as days, weeks (`W`), month ends (`ME`) or quarter ends (`QE`), including empty periods.
The change compared with the same period a year earlier, such as `pct_change(4)` on quarterly data; it removes seasonal patterns from the comparison.
A pandas function that splits values into groups of about equal size at quantiles, such as quartiles, unlike `cut`, which uses boundaries you choose.
The middle value of a sorted column, with half the values below it; in skewed data such as order values it describes a typical value better than the mean.
A number from -1 to 1 measuring how strongly two numeric columns move together in a straight-line pattern; it signals association, not cause.
An analysis that anyone can rerun from the raw files, top to bottom, with no manual steps, and get the same results, using parameters, functions and assertions.
